clue.text: How poet's day starts, absorbing French from novel

indicators.note: one piece takes in the other, so the French word sits inside the poetic morning

parts.note: morn is the poetic word for the start of the day, morning
de is the French word for from

explanation.surface: A description of how a poet begins the day, picking up some French from a novel being read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, but it is the adjective meaning new.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, novel means new or up to date, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Day to eat American beef

indicators.note: the day takes the American inside it, as if swallowing it

parts.note: Mon is the usual short form of Monday

explanation.surface: Someone sets a day for eating American beef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beef' is the verb, slang for complain, not meat.
explanation.definitionFit: To beef is slang for grumbling or complaining, a synonym of the verb here.

clue.text: Opera singer to perform part, taking 30 seconds

indicators.note: the two short verbs take the time between them, holding it

parts.note: to do is to perform
to part is to leave or go
thirty seconds is half a minute, and half of the word minute is MIN

explanation.surface: An opera singer is asked to perform a part, taking only half a minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' reads as a role, but here it is the verb meaning depart.
explanation.definitionFit: Placido Domingo is a famous Spanish tenor, an example of an opera singer.

clue.text: Dancer drops letter opener, we hear?

indicators.note: the listener hears the words spoken, so the sound is what counts

parts.note: drops falling from clouds are rain; Dear is the greeting a letter traditionally begins with

explanation.surface: A dancer lets fall the knife used to slit envelopes.
explanation.walkthrough: Dancer is one of Santa's reindeer; 'letter opener' is not a knife but the greeting Dear.
explanation.definitionFit: Dancer is the name of one of Father Christmas's sleigh-pulling animals, an example.

clue.text: Forceful politician enters — what a jerk!

indicators.note: the politician goes into the exclamation

parts.note: eh is an exclamation like what?
MP is a Member of Parliament
a tic is an involuntary jerk

explanation.surface: A forceful politician barges in, prompting someone to call them an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' reads as an insult but is a twitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Emphatic speech is strong and insistent, a synonym of forceful.

clue.text: Tramp is embracing your noble lady

parts.note: to tramp is to march

indicators.note: the word is holds the other piece in its arms

parts.note: one's is the formal pronoun for your, as in to one's credit

explanation.surface: A vagrant hugs your aristocratic wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp' looks like a noun for a vagrant but is the verb meaning walk heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: A marchioness is the wife of a marquess, a woman of noble rank.

clue.text: Perfect way to be virtuous

parts.note: to perfect a skill is to hone it
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Advice that the ideal route to goodness is a particular path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect' reads as an adjective but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An honest person is upright and truthful, a near-synonym of virtuous.

clue.text: Breaking through rickety gate, I'm going to farmland

indicators.note: the contraction forces its way into the middle of the rearranged gate
a rickety gate is falling apart, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: I'll is the contraction for I will, I'm going to

explanation.surface: Someone breaks through a shaky gate on the way into a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rickety' makes TAGE of gate, and ILL goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tillage is land under cultivation, ploughed farmland.

clue.text: Might an old man always holiday across the Atlantic?

parts.note: might, in the sense of being able, is can
an and a are both the indefinite article
old man is slang for father, dad
ay is an old word for always, usually spelt aye

explanation.surface: A question about whether an elderly man is perpetually on holiday overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: From Britain, 'across the Atlantic' points to North America.
explanation.definitionFit: Canada Day, 1 July, is Canada's national holiday, on the far side of the ocean from Britain.

clue.text: Prepare miners for war in horrid place

parts.note: to prepare for war is to arm
a pit is a coal mine, standing for the miners who work it

explanation.surface: Getting coal miners ready for battle in a dreadful spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for war' completes 'Prepare': to prepare for war is to arm.
explanation.definitionFit: An armpit is slang for a dismal, unpleasant place, as in the armpit of the country.

clue.text: Fellow standing by rebuffed love for soul queen

parts.note: standing, one's status, is rank

indicators.note: rebuffed means pushed back, so the word for zero is read backwards

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, nil

explanation.surface: A man waiting nearby is turned down in favour of a soul diva.
explanation.walkthrough: Love, a score of nothing, gives NIL, which 'rebuffed' turns into LIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Aretha Franklin was known as the Queen of Soul.

clue.text: Unabashed lad in disorderly drama

indicators.note: disorderly means out of order, so the letters of the three words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A shameless young man appears in a chaotic play.
explanation.walkthrough: Note 'in' is part of the fodder as well as the signal: the letters are those of UNABASHED LAD IN.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ideal Husband is a comedy by Oscar Wilde, an example of a drama.

clue.text: A little money to pen charming account one's added to letters

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so the outer pieces hold the inner ones

parts.note: a cent is a small coin
cute means charming

explanation.surface: Someone sets aside a small sum to write a delightful account that adds to some correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pen' is not writing but enclosing; 'letters' are characters of the alphabet, not post.
explanation.definitionFit: An acute accent is a mark placed over a character, as on the e in café.

clue.text: Writing abridged by men who'll require the accusative case?

parts.note: prose is ordinary written language
abridged means shortened, cut
OR, other ranks, is the military term for ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: A grammar puzzle about shortened text by men needing a particular Latin case.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'accusative case' is not grammar but a legal case brought by the accusing side.
explanation.definitionFit: A prosecutor presents the case against an accused person in court.

clue.text: Friend is pocketing millions before tax — this generates fortunes

parts.note: a pal is a friend
M is the abbreviation for million
to tax someone is to try or strain them

explanation.surface: A friend is stashing millions away before paying tax, which builds wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fortunes' looks like wealth but means predictions read from hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Palmistry is reading the lines of the hand to tell what the future holds.

clue.text: Flog some 7 down

indicators.note: some of means just a part of the spelled-out cross-reference is kept, its middle run

parts.note: the cross-reference is read literally, spelt out as the words seven down

explanation.surface: An instruction to sell a portion of the farmland in 7 down.
explanation.walkthrough: '7 down' is not really a cross-reference: spelt out as SEVEN DOWN, its inner run of letters (dropping SE and OWN) gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Flog is British slang for sell, and vend means to sell.

clue.text: Health service not privatised? That makes you happy

parts.note: care is health service, as in health care
a public service not privatised is free at the point of use

explanation.surface: A political point that free public healthcare keeps people content.
explanation.definitionFit: Carefree describes being untroubled and light-hearted, a near-synonym of happy.

clue.text: Main actor having field day

parts.note: a lea is a meadow or field

explanation.surface: A star performer enjoying a triumphant day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having a field day' reads as an idiom for enjoyment, but splits into field and day.
explanation.definitionFit: The lead is the principal role in a play or film, the chief actor.

clue.text: See 24
A typical Telegraph reader backs party making disclosures

indicators.note: backs means supports from behind, so the Telegraph reader comes after the party

parts.note: a revel is a lively party
the Daily Telegraph is a right-leaning British newspaper, typically read by Tories, Conservatives

explanation.surface: A newspaper reader supports a political party while revealing secrets.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Telegraph is a British newspaper associated with Conservative supporters, called Tories; 'party' is a celebration, not a political group.
explanation.definitionFit: Revelatory means revealing something previously hidden, as disclosures do.

clue.text: Reform Church of England could obstruct

indicators.note: to reform is to reshape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A claim that restructuring the Anglican church might block progress.
explanation.definitionFit: To occlude is to block or close off, a formal synonym of obstruct.

clue.text: Expert satisfied with a raise for now

parts.note: a pro is an expert

indicators.note: in a down clue a raise lifts the word upwards, reading it from bottom to top

parts.note: to have met demands is to have satisfied them

explanation.surface: A professional pleased with a pay rise, for the time being.
explanation.walkthrough: MET, from satisfied, reads TEM once 'with a raise' turns it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pro tem, short for pro tempore, is Latin for temporarily, for the time being.

clue.text: Guides use the facilities in Scottish island, it's reported

indicators.note: the guiding and the urinating go inside the island word

parts.note: inch is a Scottish word for a small island
to guide is to direct, so guides gives directs
to use the facilities is a euphemism for to urinate, pee

explanation.surface: Tour guides use the toilets on a Scottish island, so the story goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's reported' looks like a link phrase but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Indirect speech is the grammatical form for reporting what someone said, without quoting.

clue.text: Fat, heartless landowner up north

indicators.note: without a heart, the central letter of the word is removed

parts.note: a laird is a Scottish landowner, Scotland being up north

explanation.surface: A cruel, overweight landowner in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' reads as an adjective describing the landowner, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Lard is pig fat used in cooking, an example of fat.

clue.text: Ten years of life slipped away in games

indicators.note: the leaving goes inside the games

parts.note: ties are matches, games in a cup competition
went means left or slipped away

explanation.surface: A decade of life gone by while playing games.
explanation.definitionFit: Your twenties are the decade of life between ages twenty and twenty-nine.

clue.text: Bikini-clad star reads a Sun slur in shock

indicators.note: in shock means jolted, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A star in a bikini is horrified to read an insult in the Sun newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Ursula Andress famously emerged from the sea in a white bikini in the Bond film Dr No.

clue.text: A bit of practice time, so you must reverse park

indicators.note: the selected letters are read from right to left
only a part of these words is taken, running across them

explanation.surface: Driving lesson advice: a short spell of practice, then you need to reverse into a parking spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverse park' looks like a driving manoeuvre, but 'park' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Yosemite is a famous national park in California.

clue.text: Set about to finish fantastic story

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to set, as a jelly does, is to gel
to finish is to end

explanation.surface: Instructions to get going on finishing an incredible tale.
explanation.definitionFit: A legend is a traditional tale, often with marvellous or unbelievable elements.
